cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What is access control at the retrieval layer?
cards.answer: Moving authorization out of the application and into search itself: every indexed chunk carries the roles/entitlements permitted to see it, and at query time the retriever restricts candidates to chunks matching the caller's authenticated identity — so unauthorized content is never retrieved or put in the prompt.

cards.heading: Why not filter after generation
cards.question: Why is filtering a model's output after generation not a sound way to prevent unauthorized disclosure?
cards.answer: A model that has already seen a document can reveal it in forms no output filter reliably catches — a paraphrase, an aggregate, an inference — so the only durable boundary is one the unauthorized content never crosses in the first place.

cards.heading: Single enforcement point
cards.question: Why does enforcing access control at the retrieval layer cover more interfaces than application-level checks?
cards.answer: Every consuming interface — chat, agent, batch job — reaches the corpus through the same query path, so one filter at retrieval covers all of them instead of each application needing its own check.

cards.heading: Design constraints
cards.question: What three conditions does access control at the retrieval layer depend on to work correctly?
cards.answer: Entitlements captured at indexing time and re-synchronised as source permissions change (a stale tag leaks silently); identity arriving with the query rather than inferred; and a vector store that supports high-performance metadata filtering.

cards.heading: Without it
cards.question: What does an internal knowledge base's retrieval index become if access control isn't enforced there?
cards.answer: The one system that has read everything and enforces nothing — the opposite of the zero-trust-shaped foundation this technique provides.
